stem: You send the same prompt twice with the same parameters and get slightly different answers. What best explains this?

options.text: The API caches previous answers and deliberately varies them on repeat calls.
Tokens are sampled from a probability distribution, so outputs are non-deterministic.
The context window shrinks slightly between calls, changing what the model sees.
The model updates its weights from each request, so it learns between calls.

rationale: LLMs generate text one token at a time by sampling from a distribution; even with low temperature, outputs are not guaranteed to be identical.

why_wrong.A: There is no such answer cache.
why_wrong.C: The context window is a fixed model property.
why_wrong.D: Models do not update their weights from API requests.

source.excerpt: Even with temperature set to 0, the results will not be fully deterministic and identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls.

stem: A classifier keeps confusing two similar labels even with clear instructions. Which change is most likely to improve accuracy with minimal effort?

options.text: Add a few diverse labeled examples (multishot) showing the boundary between the labels.
Make the instructions longer and repeat them three times in the prompt.
Increase temperature so the model considers more candidate labels.
Ask the model to answer with only the label and no explanation.

rationale: Multishot examples demonstrate the decision boundary directly, which is usually more effective than restating instructions when categories are easily confused.

why_wrong.B: Repetition adds tokens without showing the distinction.
why_wrong.C: Higher temperature increases randomness, the opposite of what is needed.
why_wrong.D: Brevity does not address the confusion between labels.

source.excerpt: A few well-crafted examples (known as few-shot or multishot prompting) improve accuracy and consistency.

stem: A chat UI must show Claude's reply as it is being generated instead of after the full response. What should the backend use?

options.text: Polling the Messages API every second to fetch the partial results so far.
Streaming (stream: true), forwarding server-sent text deltas to the UI as they arrive.
The Message Batches API, returning each result to the UI when it is ready.
A larger max_tokens value so the full reply arrives in a single response.

rationale: Streaming delivers incremental events (such as content_block_delta) over server-sent events, which the backend can forward to the client.

why_wrong.A: The API does not expose partial results to polling.
why_wrong.C: Batches are asynchronous and the opposite of realtime.
why_wrong.D: Output length is unrelated to incremental delivery.

source.excerpt: When creating a Message, you can set "stream": true to incrementally stream the response using server-sent events (SSE).

stem: A high-volume, latency-sensitive feature extracts a few fields from short customer messages. Quality is acceptable on every tier in your evals. Which model choice best fits?

options.text: The most capable Opus-tier model, to be safe.
The fastest, lowest-cost Haiku-tier model that passes your evals.
Whichever model has the largest context window.
Rotate randomly among models to spread cost.

rationale: When evals show acceptable quality, the smallest fast model minimizes latency and cost at high volume. Capability headroom you do not need is wasted spend.

why_wrong.A: Overkill: more cost and latency without a measured gain.
why_wrong.C: Short messages do not need a large context window.
why_wrong.D: Random rotation hurts consistency and is not cost modeling.

source.excerpt: For many applications, starting with a faster, more cost-effective model like Claude Haiku 5.5 can be the optimal approach

stem: Every request to your app sends the same long system prompt and tool definitions, followed by a short, changing user question. Which technique most directly reduces cost and latency for the repeated part?

options.text: Prompt caching, with a cache_control breakpoint after the stable prefix.
Moving the system prompt to the end of the message list.
Compressing the system prompt with gzip before sending it.
Sending the tool definitions only every other request.

rationale: Prompt caching reuses a stable prefix (tools, system, earlier messages) across calls, so repeated tokens are read from cache at a lower price and with less latency.

why_wrong.B: Caching relies on an identical prefix; moving content to the end defeats it.
why_wrong.C: The API counts tokens, not bytes; compression is not supported this way.
why_wrong.D: The model would lose tool access on alternate requests.

source.excerpt: Prompt caching optimizes your API usage by allowing resuming from specific prefixes in your prompts.

options.text: Tokens are the smallest units the model processes and can map to words, subwords, characters, or bytes.
The tokenizer silently drops whitespace and punctuation before billing, inflating the billed count.
Every API call adds a fixed overhead of one thousand tokens regardless of prompt size.
Token counts are rounded up to the nearest full context window on every request.

rationale: Cost estimates based on word counts undershoot because tokenization is sub-word: one word can become several tokens, and characters or bytes can also be tokens. The team should count tokens with the model's tokenizer instead of counting words.

source.excerpt: Tokens are the smallest individual units of a language model, and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or even bytes

stem: A platform team budgets API spend by counting English words in prompts, assuming one token equals one word. Their estimates consistently undershoot the billed usage. Which statement BEST explains the mismatch?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because invisible processing sounds plausible, but tokenizers encode all text including whitespace rather than dropping it.
why_wrong.C: It tempts because fixed per-request fees exist in many APIs, but there is no fixed thousand-token surcharge per call.
why_wrong.D: It tempts by confusing the window limit with billing, but usage reflects actual tokens processed, not the window size.

options.text: Set temperature close to 0.0, which suits analytical and multiple-choice tasks needing the most probable answer.
Set temperature to its maximum so the model weighs every routing queue equally.
Alternate temperature between low and high on each retry to average out mistakes.
Omit the temperature parameter, which disables sampling entirely for classification.

rationale: Ticket routing is an analytical multiple-choice task where the most probable label is wanted every run. Temperature near 0.0 concentrates sampling on the most likely outputs, which is exactly what the requirement calls for.

source.excerpt: Use temperature closer to 0.0 for analytical / multiple choice, and closer to 1.0 for creative and generative tasks.

stem: A fintech startup uses Claude to classify support tickets into exactly one of five routing queues and needs the most consistent, probable label on every run. Which temperature setting BEST fits this requirement?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because fairness across queues sounds desirable, but maximum temperature maximizes randomness instead of consistency.
why_wrong.C: It tempts as a variance-reduction trick, but alternating temperatures just mixes deterministic and random runs without averaging anything.
why_wrong.D: It tempts because defaults feel neutral, but omitting temperature falls back to the default of 1.0 rather than disabling sampling.

options.text: Raise temperature toward 1.0 to encourage diverse outputs and surprising word choices.
Lower temperature to 0.0 so the model explores the full token distribution.
Shrink max_tokens so each description is forced into fewer, fresher words.
Resend the identical prompt repeatedly and concatenate the repeated outputs.

rationale: The studio wants varied phrasing and surprising choices, which is precisely what higher temperature provides: more creative, diverse outputs. Lowering temperature would push every description toward the same most-probable wording, the opposite of the requirement.

source.excerpt: Adjusting the temperature enables users to encourage a language model to explore rare, uncommon, or surprising word choices and sequences

stem: A game studio generates quest flavor text with Claude and complains that every tavern description reads the same despite varied prompts. They want surprising word choices and varied phrasing across generations. Which change BEST meets that requirement?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because zero sounds like a reset to full exploration, but temperature 0.0 concentrates on the most probable tokens instead.
why_wrong.C: It tempts because brevity can feel punchier, but a smaller output cap truncates text without adding any variety.
why_wrong.D: It tempts as a way to multiply content cheaply, but repeats of one deterministic-leaning output stay near-identical rather than varied.

options.text: top_k restricts sampling to only the top K candidate tokens at each step, cutting the low-probability tail.
top_p applies nucleus sampling, cutting candidates once cumulative probability reaches the threshold.
Temperature 0.0 guarantees byte-identical outputs for identical inputs on every call.
Raising top_p narrows sampling to fewer, more probable candidate tokens.
temperature and top_p must always be changed together or the API rejects the request.

rationale: top_k caps the candidate set to a fixed count per token, removing the long tail of unlikely options. top_p instead grows or shrinks the candidate set dynamically, keeping tokens until their cumulative probability reaches the threshold. Both shape the same per-token sampling distribution in complementary ways.

source.excerpt: we compute the cumulative distribution over all the options for each subsequent token in decreasing probability order

stem: A search team is tuning sampling parameters for a code-completion endpoint. Select TWO statements that correctly describe how the sampling parameters work.

why_wrong.C: It tempts because zero randomness sounds fully deterministic, but the docs state results are not fully deterministic even at temperature 0.0.
why_wrong.D: It tempts by confusing the direction of the cutoff, but a higher top_p admits more of the distribution rather than narrowing it.
why_wrong.E: It tempts because both knobs affect sampling, but each is an independent optional parameter with no joint-change requirement.

options.text: Replace exact-match assertions with property checks, since identical inputs can still yield different outputs.
Set temperature to a negative value to force fully deterministic generation in tests.
Double max_tokens so the model has room to reproduce the exact expected string.
Pin temperature at 1.0, which is the deterministic setting meant for test environments.

rationale: Even at temperature 0.0 the API is not fully deterministic, so asserting byte equality on free-form answers is inherently flaky. Property-based checks validate what actually matters, such as schema, labels, or cited values, while tolerating legitimate phrasing variation.

source.excerpt: Even with temperature set to 0, the results will not be fully deterministic and identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls.

stem: A team's CI suite asserts exact string equality on Claude's answers with temperature set to 0, and the tests fail intermittently on wording differences. Which fix BEST addresses the root cause?

why_wrong.B: It tempts as going below zero for extra determinism, but temperature ranges from 0.0 to 1.0 and negatives are invalid.
why_wrong.C: It tempts because truncation can corrupt outputs, but the failures are wording variation, which extra output room cannot prevent.
why_wrong.D: It tempts by recasting the default as the safe choice, but 1.0 is the high-randomness end of the range, not a deterministic mode.

options.text: Swap in diverse examples covering edge cases like customs holds so no unintended pattern is learned.
Add twelve more successful-delivery examples to reinforce the dominant pattern further.
Delete all examples and rely on a longer written description of the schema instead.
Raise the temperature so formatting varies enough to cover exceptions by chance.

rationale: Few-shot examples steer output format, but a one-sided set teaches the model that exceptions do not exist. Diverse examples covering edge cases show the model how each case should be formatted, which directly fixes the misformatted exceptions.

source.excerpt: Diverse: Cover edge cases and vary enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns.

stem: A logistics company prompts Claude to normalize delivery-status updates into a strict JSON schema. The prompt includes six examples, but all six show successful deliveries, and the model now misformats exceptions like customs holds. Which change is MOST likely to fix the formatting of exceptions?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because more examples usually help, but more of the same skewed pattern only deepens the bias against exceptions.
why_wrong.C: It tempts as removing the bias at its source, but dropping examples discards the most reliable formatting signal the model has.
why_wrong.D: It tempts because randomness produces variety, but random variation breaks strict schemas rather than teaching the exception format.

options.text: Raise max_tokens to fit both thinking and the answer, and budget for thinking billed as output.
Disable thinking and lower max_tokens to squeeze the same analysis into fewer tokens.
Move to a larger-window model so thinking tokens stop counting toward max_tokens.
Split the job into parallel calls that share a single max_tokens budget.

rationale: Thinking tokens consume the same max_tokens budget as the response, so a budget sized for the answer alone truncates before the final text appears. Raising max_tokens leaves room for both phases, and the higher spend is expected because reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens.

source.excerpt: Thinking tokens count toward max_tokens, so set it high enough to leave room for both the thinking and the response text.

stem: A data team runs a long agentic analysis job with thinking enabled and sees responses cut off with a max_tokens stop before the final answer appears. Token spend also rose sharply versus the non-thinking baseline. Which approach BEST addresses both symptoms?

why_wrong.B: It tempts as the cheapest fix, but dropping thinking sacrifices the intermediate reasoning that complex analysis depends on.
why_wrong.C: It tempts because a bigger window holds more context, but thinking still counts toward max_tokens regardless of window size.
why_wrong.D: It tempts as dividing the cost across workers, but max_tokens is enforced per request, not pooled across parallel calls.

options.text: Run small refactors at low effort and reserve max effort for the hunt, testing max before broad use.
Run everything at max effort so even simple refactors get the deepest reasoning available.
Run the vulnerability hunt at low effort to save tokens and refactors at max for safety.
Ignore effort controls and use temperature alone to separate quick from deep work.

rationale: Low effort fits quick, human-reviewed changes like renames, while max effort suits hard autonomous problems like vulnerability hunting. Because max can overthink with diminishing returns, it should be validated on the security workload before broad adoption rather than applied blindly everywhere.

source.excerpt: Quick exchanges where you review each result, such as brainstorming, a first sketch, or a small change like a rename

stem: An engineering org runs two Claude Code workloads: high-volume small refactors such as renames, each reviewed line by line, plus a quarterly hunt for security vulnerabilities. Which effort strategy BEST matches each workload to its need?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because more reasoning sounds strictly better, but max effort on trivial edits wastes tokens and risks overthinking.
why_wrong.C: It tempts as frugal allocation, but it starves the hard security problem of reasoning while overspending on trivial edits.
why_wrong.D: It tempts by collapsing two knobs into one, but temperature controls randomness, not reasoning depth, so it cannot substitute for effort.

options.text: The context window is the text the model can look back on, acting as its working memory.
Retained thinking blocks count as input like any other conversation history.
The context window includes the full pretraining corpus, so all training data is in context.
Raising temperature expands the context window since more candidates stay in memory.
Any request exceeding the window is always rejected with a validation error first.

rationale: The context window is the model's working memory: the prior text it can reference while generating, distinct from training data. On keep-all models, preserved thinking blocks occupy that same window as ordinary history, so long agentic sessions must budget for them.

source.excerpt: the amount of text a language model can look back on and reference when generating new text

stem: A team designing a long-running support agent debates how the context window behaves. Select TWO correct statements.

why_wrong.C: It tempts by conflating training with context, but the window is explicitly different from the training corpus.
why_wrong.D: It tempts by mixing sampling with memory, but temperature controls randomness and has no effect on window size.
why_wrong.E: It tempts because oversized requests can error, but newer models accept the request and stop mid-generation instead of always rejecting it.

options.text: Use adaptive thinking so the model scales reasoning depth to each request's complexity.
Set a large fixed thinking budget on every request so simple lookups get extra reasoning.
Disable thinking entirely and compensate with higher temperature on complex traces.
Route all traffic at max effort to guarantee uniform reasoning depth everywhere.

rationale: Whether and how deeply Claude thinks depends on the request's complexity, and adaptive thinking exploits exactly that: simple lookups get light reasoning while debugging traces get deep reasoning. A fixed budget or uniform max effort would burn tokens on requests that do not need them.

source.excerpt: Whether Claude thinks on a given request, and how deeply, depends on your thinking configuration and the complexity of the request.

stem: A SaaS company routes mixed traffic through one endpoint: simple FAQ lookups and occasional multi-step debugging traces. They want deep reasoning only when a request warrants it, without hand-tuning a thinking budget per request. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?

why_wrong.B: It tempts because a big budget never under-thinks, but it wastes billed reasoning tokens on lookups that need almost none.
why_wrong.C: It tempts as trading one knob for another, but temperature adds randomness, not the step-by-step reasoning complex traces need.
why_wrong.D: It tempts through uniformity, but uniform max effort overspends on simple traffic and risks overthinking.

options.text: POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with a JSON body holding model and messages.
GET https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with the prompt passed as a query string value.
POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/models with a JSON body holding model and messages.
PUT https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with the conversation encoded as XML in the body.

rationale: The Claude API is RESTful at api.anthropic.com and conversational requests go to POST /v1/messages with a JSON body. GET cannot carry a message payload, the models endpoint lists models instead of chatting, and the API expects JSON rather than XML.

source.excerpt: Messages API : Send messages to Claude for conversational interactions ( POST /v1/messages )

stem: A startup is integrating Claude over raw HTTPS without an SDK. A backend developer must send the first conversational request to the model. Which request correctly targets the Messages API?

why_wrong.B: Query strings look simple, but the Messages endpoint requires a POST carrying a JSON body.
why_wrong.C: The models endpoint is real, but it lists available models instead of running a conversation.
why_wrong.D: PUT resembles a write call, but this API uses POST with JSON rather than XML.

options.text: Authorization bearer key, anthropic-version, and content-type application/json.
x-request-id, anthropic-version, and accept-encoding gzip on each call.
Authorization bearer key and user-agent only, with versioning negotiated.
content-type application/json and cache-control no-cache, with the key in the URL.

rationale: Direct API requests must carry authentication, the anthropic-version header, and content-type application/json, while a single-workspace key needs no workspace header. Request IDs travel in responses, versioning is a required header rather than negotiation, and keys belong in headers rather than URLs.

source.excerpt: | anthropic-version | API version (for example, 2023-06-01 ) | Yes |

stem: A developer's raw curl call to POST /v1/messages fails because required headers are missing. The team uses a standard single-workspace API key. Which header set makes the request valid?

why_wrong.B: Request IDs appear in API traffic, but they are returned in responses rather than required on requests.
why_wrong.C: Bearer auth alone looks sufficient, but the API also requires the version and content-type headers.
why_wrong.D: A URL key seems convenient, but credentials belong in headers and the version header is missing.

options.text: Send the request with stream true and consume the SSE event flow of deltas.
Open a WebSocket channel and subscribe to a token topic per session.
Poll the created message every 200 ms until a stop reason appears.
Open two parallel non-streaming calls and interleave their paragraphs.

rationale: The Messages API streams incrementally over server-sent events when stream is true, emitting deltas the client forwards to the UI. The API offers no WebSocket token channel, polling cannot fetch partial output, and parallel full responses still arrive only when complete.

source.excerpt: When creating a Message, you can set "stream": true to incrementally stream the response using server-sent events (SSE).

stem: A team building a live coding assistant debates transports: one engineer proposes opening a WebSocket to api.anthropic.com for token-by-token output, another proposes SSE. The assistant must render each token as it arrives. Which approach best fits the Messages API?

why_wrong.B: WebSockets suit bidirectional chat apps, but this API delivers streaming output over SSE rather than sockets.
why_wrong.C: Polling works for job queues, but the API exposes no partial-result endpoint to poll.
why_wrong.D: Parallelism speeds up batches, but two full responses still arrive only when complete.

options.text: Mid-stream error events can arrive after a 200, so handle error events and fail over.
SSE streams always complete after a 200, so the hang must be a rendering bug.
The API buffers the full reply first, so the fix is raising the client timeout.
Streaming needs a second call to close, so the client must re-POST each stream.

rationale: Over SSE, an error such as overloaded_error can occur after the API already returned HTTP 200, so status-code checks alone miss it. The consumer must listen for error events and surface retries or fallback UI instead of waiting forever for a final message.

source.excerpt: When receiving a streaming response over server-sent events (SSE), an error can occur after the API returns a 200 response

stem: A support-chat backend consumes the SSE stream and assumes any HTTP 200 means success. During a traffic spike some streams die halfway with no final message and the UI hangs. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?

why_wrong.B: Trusting the 200 status is natural for REST, but SSE pushes errors inside the stream after headers are sent.
why_wrong.C: Timeouts cause hangs elsewhere, but here the documented failure is an in-stream error event, not buffering.
why_wrong.D: A closing handshake exists in some protocols, but this stream ends with message_stop or an error event.

options.text: Use the SDK streaming call and collect the final message, keeping the link alive via SSE.
Split every request into single-sentence calls and concatenate the texts afterwards.
Raise max_tokens further so each response finishes in fewer round trips.
Poll the Token Counting API until the full generated text is ready.

rationale: The SDK can stream internally while returning the complete Message object identical to create, which is the documented remedy for large-max_tokens requests where streaming avoids HTTP timeouts. Sentence-splitting adds round trips, larger limits worsen timeouts, and token counting never returns text.

source.excerpt: where the SDK requires streaming to avoid HTTP timeouts

stem: A report generator requests very long outputs with a large max_tokens value and intermittently fails with HTTP timeouts on non-streaming calls. The team does not need incremental rendering. Which change best fixes the timeouts?

why_wrong.B: Chunking helps some limits, but dozens of round trips add latency when streaming already solves the timeout.
why_wrong.C: Bigger limits sound like fewer calls, but longer generations make non-streaming timeouts more likely.
why_wrong.D: The counting endpoint manages budgets, but it returns token counts and never generated text.

options.text: Automatic management of authentication, version, and content-type headers.
Built-in retry logic with exponential backoff for transient failures.
Lower latency because SDK calls use a dedicated fast endpoint.
Automatic prompt rewriting that trims token usage.
A stable response schema that stays the same across API versions.

rationale: The SDKs simplify integration by handling authentication, request formatting, and error handling, including automatic headers and built-in retries with backoff. They still call the same API with the same latency, never rewrite prompts, and response shapes may expand over time.

source.excerpt: Anthropic provides official SDKs that simplify API integration by handling authentication, request formatting, error handling, and more.

stem: A platform team must decide whether new microservices should call the Messages API through raw HTTP or the official client SDKs. Which TWO advantages do the official SDKs provide over hand-rolled HTTP? Select TWO.

why_wrong.C: A local library feels faster, but every SDK call still travels to the same API with the same latency.
why_wrong.D: Token savings are attractive, but no SDK rewrites prompts or guarantees usage cuts.
why_wrong.E: Stability is desirable, but the versioning policy allows response objects to expand.

options.text: Accumulate the partial JSON string deltas and parse once content_block_stop arrives.
Parse each fragment independently and merge the resulting objects by key order.
Disable streaming for tool use and require the model to emit XML instead.
Request one token per stream event so every fragment parses as valid JSON.

rationale: Tool-use deltas carry partial JSON strings while only the final input is a complete object, so the documented pattern is accumulating string deltas and parsing after content_block_stop, optionally with partial-JSON helpers. Fragments are not standalone objects, XML is unrelated, and one-token events are still fragments.

source.excerpt: You can accumulate the string deltas and parse the JSON once you receive a content_block_stop event

stem: An agent harness streams tool calls and tries to JSON-parse each input_json_delta fragment as it arrives, throwing parse errors on every long tool call. The tool input must still be captured completely. What should the harness do instead?

why_wrong.B: Merging sounds incremental, but fragments are arbitrary string slices that cannot parse alone.
why_wrong.C: Non-streaming avoids the bug, but it discards streaming instead of fixing the accumulation logic.
why_wrong.D: Smaller events seem cleaner, but each fragment remains a partial string rather than valid JSON.

options.text: Catch the SDK typed exceptions such as NotFoundError, most specific classes first.
Keep string-matching messages but pin the SDK version forever to freeze wording.
Catch only the base Exception and retry every failure exactly three times.
Parse the HTTP status out of the message text with a regex on each error.

rationale: The SDK raises typed exceptions instead of raw JSON, and the documented practice is catching those classes with the most specific first rather than string-matching messages that can change. Pinning freezes wording but blocks fixes, blind retries waste budget on permanent errors, and regex parsing reintroduces the same fragility.

source.excerpt: Catch the SDK's typed classes rather than string-matching error messages, handling the most specific classes first.

stem: A Python service catches every API failure with a broad except Exception and string-matches messages like 'not found' to decide retries. After an SDK upgrade the matching silently breaks. Which error-handling approach is most robust?

why_wrong.B: Pinning feels safe, but it blocks security fixes while message text can still evolve.
why_wrong.C: Uniform retries look simple, but they waste budget on permanent errors like bad requests.
why_wrong.D: Regex extraction seems precise, but it depends on the same unstable message wording.

options.text: Back off exponentially honoring retry-after, cap attempts, and shrink 413 payloads instead of retrying.
Keep retrying immediately but raise the cap to fifty attempts so each request finally succeeds.
Retry every status on a fixed one-second interval and ignore retry-after to stay uniform.
Disable retries entirely and fail each request on its first error to shield the API.

rationale: The SDK default retries transient failures such as rate limits and 5xx with backoff, twice by default, honoring retry-after, with max_retries to cap attempts; a 413 means the request exceeds size limits and needs a smaller payload rather than retries. Aggressive or uniform retries amplify overload, while zero retries turn transient blips into user-facing errors.

source.excerpt: retries transient failures (such as connection errors, rate limits, and 5xx server errors) with exponential backoff, twice by default

stem: During an overload incident, a high-traffic service retries every failed Messages call immediately up to ten times. Logs show 529s, 429s with retry-after headers, and 413s from oversized payloads; the retry storm deepens the outage. Which retry policy best resolves the incident?

why_wrong.B: More attempts feel thorough, but immediate retries during overload multiply load and prolong the outage.
why_wrong.C: Fixed intervals look fair, but ignoring retry-after disobeys the server's explicit pacing signal.
why_wrong.D: Zero retries protect capacity, but they convert recoverable 529s and 429s into avoidable failures.

options.text: Ignore unknown event types gracefully so newly added events never crash the parser.
Handle in-stream error events because failures can arrive after HTTP 200.
Reject any stream whose first event is not message_stop to fail fast.
Require an exact event count per response and abort streams that deviate.
Cache the first stream forever and replay it for later requests.

rationale: New event types may be added, so code must handle unknown types gracefully, and errors can arrive inside the stream after a 200, so error events need explicit handling. Streams open with message_start rather than message_stop, delta counts legitimately vary with output length, and replaying stale streams fabricates responses.

source.excerpt: new event types may be added, and your code should handle unknown event types gracefully.

stem: A team is hardening an SSE consumer that processes the Messages event flow for a production dashboard. Which TWO practices make the consumer robust to API evolution and stream failures? Select TWO.

why_wrong.C: Failing fast is healthy, but message_stop closes the stream while the opening event is message_start.
why_wrong.D: Exact counts look strict, but delta counts legitimately vary with output length.
why_wrong.E: Replay avoids API calls, but serving a cached stream as a fresh answer fabricates data.

options.text: Send the authentication, anthropic-version, and content-type headers on each request.
Read rate-limit responses and wait out retry-after before retrying when present.
Open a persistent WebSocket to api.anthropic.com for all inference calls.
Embed the API key in the URL query string for audit logging.
Skip response validation because raw HTTP responses never carry errors.

rationale: Without the SDK, the hand-rolled client must send the auth, version, and content-type headers itself, and when a 429 carries retry-after it must wait that many seconds before retrying. Inference runs over REST and SSE rather than WebSockets, keys belong in headers rather than URLs, and JSON error bodies always need handling.

source.excerpt: the SDK sends the authentication, version, and content-type headers automatically

stem: A government contractor must call the Messages API over hand-rolled HTTP because third-party SDK packages are banned. Which TWO requirements must their hand-rolled client satisfy? Select TWO.

why_wrong.C: Sockets fit push workloads, but this API serves inference over REST and SSE rather than WebSockets.
why_wrong.D: URLs are easy to log, but that leaks credentials while keys belong in request headers.
why_wrong.E: Skipping validation saves code, but every failure arrives as JSON that callers must handle.
